title: Solidarity
hook: stub a toe and the whole body stops: Paul's picture, stretched to the whole human race

segments.voice: Yesterday, the carpenter of Nazareth and the dignity of work. Your line was work has dignity. Did a worker hear thanks for the work itself? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-eight.

Stub a toe on the bed frame at night, and the whole body stops. Hands reach down. The face winces. A word comes out that wouldn't be said in church. Nobody called a meeting. Paul uses that picture, writing to the Christians at Corinth about how they belong to each other. In the Douay-Rheims: "if one member suffer any thing, all the members suffer with it; or if one member glory, all the members rejoice with it." Catholic social teaching takes that picture of one body and stretches it past the church door, to the whole human race. Today, solidarity.
screen: `A STUBBED TOE STOPS THE BODY.` → `IF ONE MEMBER SUFFER.` → `PAST THE CHURCH DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, the ground of it. In Acts, Paul stands before the council in Athens, among people whose gods are not his, and tells them, in the Douay-Rheims, that God "hath made of one, all mankind, to dwell upon the whole face of the earth." Made of one. Catholic teaching reads that as one human family, whatever the borders, languages or religions. Second, what solidarity is not. John Paul the Second wrote that it isn't a feeling of vague pity at the troubles of people far away. It's a firm, lasting commitment to the common good, to the good of all and of each, because everyone is responsible for everyone. A feeling passes when the news changes. A commitment keeps showing up. Third, how close the far-off already is. The shirt on your back was sewn somewhere. The coffee was picked by someone. Lives on opposite sides of the earth are already tied together. Solidarity asks that those ties be just, that the person at the other end of the thread is treated as family. Paul puts the daily version to the Galatians: "Bear ye one another's burdens." Fourth, it runs both ways. Look again at Paul's line. When one member suffers, all suffer; when one member is honored, all rejoice. Solidarity isn't only pity flowing downhill. It's also learning from, celebrating with, and receiving from people far away. One family shares the grief and the feast.
screen: `MADE OF ONE.` · `NOT VAGUE PITY, A COMMITMENT.` · then, large: `BEAR YE ONE ANOTHER'S BURDENS.` · then: `IT RUNS BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a far-off people in your heart. Settle, and breathe. Choose a place far from you. A country in the news this week. The place your clothes were sewn. A region you know almost nothing about. Let it be real people, not a map: someone waking up there, cooking, worrying about a child, laughing at something. If you pray, you can pray for them, as Catholics do in the prayers of the faithful at Mass. If you don't, just hold them in mind, as family you haven't met. The bell holds the time.
Solidarity. One human family, made of one, where one member's pain and joy belong to all, held as a firm commitment, not a passing feeling. Today's word.
Your line: one family. Today, when news from far away comes on, picture one person there as a cousin you haven't met yet. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for people around the world in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, and some parishes support relief and development work abroad, sometimes through partnerships with a parish in another country.

fork.reveal: "hath made of one, all mankind." Paul starts with what he and the Athenians share before anything that divides them.

original.note: Greek: body. Paul's word for the many members that suffer and rejoice together.

notes: Confirm the Douay-Rheims wording of Acts 17:26 ('And hath made of one, all mankind, to dwell upon the whole face of the earth').
Sollicitudo Rei Socialis 38 paraphrased (solidarity as 'a firm and persevering determination to commit oneself to the common good'); the Vatican English is not quoted.
'Solidarity runs both ways' draws on the second half of 1 Corinthians 12:26 and is an interpretive emphasis; confirm.
